name: Dog domestication, Late Pleistocene Eurasia
summary: At Bonn-Oberkassel, Late Pleistocene people buried a young dog with two humans. The dog’s repeated illness suggests it may have received human care.
description: At Bonn-Oberkassel in Germany, a young domestic dog was buried with two humans. Tooth enamel records repeated illness that, according to Janssens and colleagues, the animal was unlikely to survive without care. The timing and place of initial dog domestication remain open.

impact.note: Scored on the general view, not on the cited paper, that later dogs descend from Late Pleistocene Eurasian domestication and came to live with people on every inhabited continent; a hunting, guarding and hauling partner was a new capability, and a few later lines such as herding and sled dogs built on it.

date.label: c. 12,290-12,050 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Four radiocarbon dates on the bones of the Bonn-Oberkassel dog fall between about 12,900 and 11,850 cal BCE, with a weighted mean between 12,290 and 12,050 cal BCE.

evidence.supports: Four radiocarbon dates were performed on the canine bones (for details see Table 3), situating them between ca. 12900/12850 and ca. 11900/11850 cal BC. Their weighted mean is between 12290 and 12050 cal BC

date.label: c. 12,290-12,050 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The authors call the two dogs of the Bonn-Oberkassel burial some of the oldest undisputed evidence for domestic dogs; the date given here is that of the younger dog, from the dating section, not from this passage.

evidence.supports: These two late Pleistocene Bonn-Oberkassel dogs provide some of the oldest undisputed evidence for domestic dogs.

earliest_record.rationale: Dates the directly measured Bonn-Oberkassel specimen. The dated evidence for dog presence at other sites is a separate question.

unresolved.note: New directly dated genomes document dogs at Pınarbaşı and Gough’s Cave. They do not locate domestication or show a connection to Bonn-Oberkassel. Find earlier directly dated remains and geographically informative ancestry patterns to resolve the domestication region and any direction of exchange.

evidence.locator: pp. 996–997, Dogs were widespread during the Palaeolithic; Fig. 1
evidence.supports: Nuclear DNA assigns the directly dated canids from Pınarbaşı and Gough’s Cave to dogs. The study gives a distinct date range for each specimen.

research.note: Marsh and colleagues document earlier dogs in western Eurasia. The dated events here concern the Bonn-Oberkassel burial.

caveats: This record dates the evidence at Bonn-Oberkassel. Directly dated ancient DNA identifies dogs at Pınarbaşı in Anatolia (15,915–15,669 cal BP) and at Gough’s Cave in Britain (14,793–14,090 cal BP). Their relationship to the Bonn-Oberkassel community remains unresolved.
